title: Mike Rogers' Real Record: What He Says Now vs. How He Actually Voted
script: This is Michigan's Mike Rogers — he represented Michigan's 8th District in the House from 2001 to 2015, and chaired the House Intelligence Committee. He is not the other Mike Rogers, the congressman from Alabama. Mike Rogers is asking Michigan for a promotion to the United States Senate — and he is asking you to judge him on what he says in 2026, not on what he did in fourteen years in Congress. So tonight, Current Bureau does the opposite. Every claim in the next eight minutes comes with a bill number, a roll-call vote, or a fact-checker's verdict. This is Mike Rogers' real record — in his own words, and then in his own votes. Start with prescription drugs, on the Detroit River, this July. Rogers looked across at Windsor, Canada, and said — quote — 'I'll make sure that you don't have to pay any more for your prescription than they do in Canada.' End quote. Here is what he did when he had the power. In 2003, he voted yes on the Medicare law, H.R. 1, that barred Medicare from negotiating drug prices at all. In 2007, he voted no — Roll Call 23 — on H.R. 4, the bill that would have let Medicare negotiate. And Bridge Michigan's fact-checkers found he voted at least four times against letting cheaper drugs be reimported from Canada — the very country in his ad. Their verdict on that record: largely true. PolitiFact calls the wider pattern — five votes against Medicare negotiation — generally accurate. He is now running on the price gap he voted, again and again, to keep open. And when negotiation finally became law, years after he left, he called it — quote — 'sugar high politics,' and said he is passionately against it. Second: reproductive freedom. Michigan voters wrote it into their state constitution in 2022, by thirteen points. This weekend, Rogers pledged — quote — 'I will never go to Washington and overturn the will of the Michigan people.' Here is the record that pledge has to carry. In 2013, he voted yes on H.R. 1797, Roll Call 251 — a nationwide ban on abortion after twenty weeks. Federal law beats state constitutions; that vote was a vote to override states exactly like Michigan. He co-sponsored four bills granting legal personhood from the moment of fertilization, and bills in 2003 and 2005 to pull FDA approval of the abortion medication mifepristone. Now he also says — quote — 'I oppose any and all efforts to restrict access to IVF, period.' Law professor Mary Ziegler's answer, on the record: you can be for IVF, or you can be for fetal personhood — you can't be for both. Rogers has never explained how his bills and his new promise fit together. CatholicVote suspended its endorsement of him over the new pledge. Reproductive Freedom for All answered with his votes. Both sides are looking at the same record. So should you. Third: affordability — his campaign's own word. His record: no on the Affordable Care Act in 2010, Roll Call 165. Yes to repealing it in 2011, and again in 2013. And this March, in a private room in Macomb County, asked about health costs, he said a fifty-dollar charge for an annual physical — a visit the ACA made free — would be, quote, 'probably okay, right?' That idea is not in his public plan, and his campaign won't say if he still holds it. One more, because it says a lot. This September his campaign posted a tribute to a firefighter who got cancer at Ground Zero. In 2010, Rogers voted no — twice, Roll Calls 491 and 550 — on the James Zadroga Act, the law that treats responders like that firefighter. The tribute is new. The votes are forever. Now the other half of his campaign: what he says about his opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. We checked every major attack with the fact-checkers. One: that El-Sayed believes America deserved 9/11. PolitiFact: Pants on Fire. Those were a streamer's words from 2019. El-Sayed said the opposite, on NBC: America didn't deserve 9/11. Two: that El-Sayed, quote, 'didn't disavow' the Muslim Brotherhood. PolitiFact: False. At a town hall in Caro, asked directly, he answered, 'Sure. Yeah, absolutely.' Rogers was shown that clip on CNN — and said, 'No, that's not true.' Three: that El-Sayed pledged support to the Brotherhood. Bridge Michigan found no evidence — the letter Rogers cites was signed by forty-six Egyptian-Americans urging Egypt's elected president to act against the old regime's allies. Four: the attack on El-Sayed's birth mother. Michigan Public's fact-check: she was a nurse in a Kenyan orphanage; she appears in no indictment; the charity's case was about sanctions violations. Five: that El-Sayed wants to ban gas-powered cars. Bridge Michigan: False — he opposed an EV mandate and said Michigan should keep building combustion engines. Six: 'defund the police and empty the prisons' as his platform today: Mostly False, says PolitiFact. Detroit's Metro Times finally stopped asking the Rogers campaign for comment at all, citing — their words — 'lies and bigoted attacks.' Those are documented verdicts, with names and dates. That is what the word means in this programme: not an insult — a record. And when words weren't enough, there were pictures that never happened. USA Today, reporting the Wesleyan Media Project's tracking, documents an AI-generated ad from Rogers' side showing El-Sayed hiding in a Trojan horse under a banner reading, 'Definitely NOT Communism.' It never occurred. Researchers call the genre 'slopaganda'; of the AI ads counted through mid-October, only about a quarter even carried a disclaimer. His biggest allied group, the Senate Leadership Fund, also built a website dressed as a Michigan news outlet — 'Trusted reporting for the state of Michigan' — with its ownership in tiny print at the bottom. One more picture deserves an honest label. In June, an AI-altered photo of Rogers himself, with exaggerated muscularity, was posted on X and flagged by the platform: Made with AI. It was posted by a woman the campaign says was not staff, and who continued to speak for the campaign. We state it exactly that way, because attribution matters in this programme. Now follow the money, from the FEC. El-Sayed's campaign out-raised Rogers' campaign, fifty-three point eight million to twenty-three million. But outside groups delivered one hundred and seventy-one million dollars of benefit to Rogers — one hundred and thirty-four million of it spent attacking El-Sayed, not presenting Rogers. One allied group spent forty-seven million alone. A group calling itself Democrats for Mike Rogers spent five point seven million — against receipts of eighty-four thousand. When there is no record for the people to run on, the attack is not part of the campaign. The attack is the campaign. Even his strongest issue moved. Trump's tariffs were 'masterful,' an 'absolute win'; Michiganders worried about prices were told the shoe was going to pinch. In the final weeks, Canadian tariffs became 'problematic' and due for a postponement. Same tariffs. New audience math. Michigan decides on Tuesday whether the Senate gets the rhetoric — or remembers the record. The record is public. The votes have numbers. And now, so does this programme. Before you go — subscribe to Current Bureau. Hit the subscribe button below this video, because this series is not done. More is coming. The Real Record series continues — more candidates, more roll calls, more receipts — before the polls close on Tuesday. And we will end on this hope: that very soon, we can celebrate together the day this kind of rhetoric and nonsense is finally out of our politics — and only the record is left. I'm Current Bureau. The record is public. Go and check it — and we'll see you in the next one.
